card.ask.value_missing_via: How big is the Fed's move? Write it in basis points.
card.ask.value_ambiguous: Is “{text}” {first} or {second}? Some countries use the point for thousands and others for decimals.
card.ask.value_unreadable: I couldn't read the value “{text}” for {input}. Write it as a number.
card.ask.driver_periods: Do you change {input} for next year only, or for every forecast year?
card.ask.method_unknown: Warren computes the terminal value with its own method or with Gordon's; it has no exit-multiple method. Which one do you want?
card.note.corte_default: Cutoff date: {date}. Warren uses only what was published up to that day, the last one that has ended in New York (today is {today}). You can pick an earlier date to see what was known then.
card.note.corte_from_question: Cutoff date: {date}, the one I read in your question. Please confirm it.
card.note.fed_move_is_event: The value is the Fed's move, not the risk-free rate's. Warren turns it into a change in the 10-year Treasury yield with a range from published studies, never one for one.
card.note.cash_unchanged: You change only the shares outstanding: the cash that would be paid or received stays the same. So value per share moves without anyone paying or receiving anything, which does not happen in real life. For a buyback, change debt: Warren adjusts the shares with it.
card.note.wacc_bypasses_parts: With WACC set directly, Warren stops using its components: beta, the risk-free rate, the equity risk premium, the cost of debt, the tax shield and the weights of debt and equity.
card.note.usd_only: Warren reports in US dollars, as these companies file their financial statements. It doesn't convert currencies.
card.note.intrinsic_value_offer: Warren doesn't forecast prices or say whether to buy. I'll show you its intrinsic value, its range and which assumptions it depends on.
card.note.intrinsic_value_offer_target: Warren doesn't compute a target price or say whether to buy. I'll show you its intrinsic value, its range and which assumptions it depends on.
input.debt_tax_rate: the tax rate on the debt tax shield
card.ask.value_currency: You wrote “{text}” in another currency. Warren doesn't convert currencies: write the amount in US dollars.
card.ask.percent_or_points: You wrote “{text}” for {input}. Is that percentage points (say, from 20% to 10%) or a share of its level (from 20% to 18%)?
card.ask.points_or_bp: You wrote “{text}” for {input}. Is that percentage points or basis points (100 bp = 1 point)?
card.ask.fed_surprise: Does the Fed's move surprise the market, or was it expected? What was expected is already in the bond yield on the cutoff date and barely moves it; only the unexpected part does.
card.ask.wacc_and_parts: You set WACC and also change one of its components. With WACC fixed, that change would have no effect. Which do you want to use?
card.note.relative_change: I read “{text}” as a relative change in {input}: a share of its current level, not percentage points.

answer.sure.title: How sure?
answer.coverage.all: of the ranges held the actual figure (8 companies)
answer.coverage.company: of {company}'s ranges held the actual figure
answer.sure.body: Each case is a one-quarter forecast Warren made on a past date, compared later with the figure the company reported. A p10–p90 range (10th to 90th percentile) should hold the actual figure about 8 times in 10. These shares are not the chance that this forecast is right: they say whether the ranges are as wide as they should be. A little over 80% means they are a little wider than needed. The forecast uses only the company's filings, not recent news.
answer.chart.title: Reported and forecast
answer.chart.aria: {company} quarterly revenue in US$ millions: {reported} reported quarters and {forecast} forecast with their p10–p90 range. The forecasts and their ranges are in the table.
answer.chart.source: Source: Warren's baseline forecast, estimate of {date}. Revenue reported in {company}'s 10-K and 10-Q filed by that date. Range: the same forecast's past misses, known on that date. Estimate:
formula.revenue_from_growth_vs_year_earl: revenue of the same quarter a year earlier (B), times (1 + the average annual growth of the last three fiscal years, C). It is Warren's baseline forecast, not the DCF.

answer.fuente.not_recorded: This estimate did not store its source.
answer.fuente.same_filing: Each growth rate uses both years as one filing reports them, so the figures are measured the same way. US$ millions.
answer.fuente.range_how: the forecast times (1 + the miss percentile), from the misses this same forecast made in the past across the 8 companies at the same number of quarters ahead ({n} misses).
answer.fuente.range_known: Misses known on {date}, from actual figures filed by {filed_to}.
answer.fuente.range_foot: The range shows how far the baseline forecast has missed before; it does not include news or other shocks, so it is not the whole uncertainty.

answer.table.season: Each forecast starts from the same quarter a year earlier, so the company's seasons stay: its biggest quarter stays on top.

refusal.code.as_of_too_early: Warren computes estimates only from {supported_from}, and your question's cut-off date is {as_of}.

refusal.code.history_too_short: Warren needs {needed} fiscal years of {empresa}'s revenue published by the cut-off date, and on {fecha} it finds {found}: {years}.
refusal.code.history_too_short.none: Warren needs {needed} fiscal years of {empresa}'s revenue published by the cut-off date, and on {fecha} it finds none.
refusal.code.too_few_comparatives: For revenue growth, Warren compares each year with the one before as a single annual report presents them, and needs {needed} such comparisons; on {fecha}, {empresa}'s reports give {found}.
refusal.code.too_few_quarters: For the Q{quarter} operating margin, Warren averages the Q{quarter}s reported in the last {window} quarters and needs at least {needed}; on {fecha}, {empresa}'s filings give {found}.
refusal.code.no_price_on_date: Warren found no price for {empresa} on {fecha} or the days before.
refusal.code.too_few_return_weeks: For beta, Warren compares {needed} weeks of {empresa}'s returns with the S&P 500's before the cut-off date, and on {fecha} there are only {found}.
refusal.code.erp_too_few_years: To estimate the market risk premium, Warren needs at least {min_years} years of annual returns, and on {fecha} it only has {first_year} to {last_year}. From {first_as_of} it has enough.
refusal.code.as_of_in_future: {as_of} hasn't ended in New York yet (today is {today}). Warren uses only days that have closed.
refusal.code.market_data_not_refreshed: Warren doesn't have prices for {fecha} yet: it has the three market series this estimate uses (the stock price, the S&P 500 and the 10-year Treasury rate) only up to {through}, so that is the newest date it can use.
refusal.code.market_data_not_refreshed.o: Warren doesn't have prices for {fecha} yet: one of the market series this estimate uses only reaches {through}.
refusal.code.seed_quarter_not_reported: The estimate starts from the last four quarters' revenue, and {empresa}'s filings published up to {fecha} don't include Q{quarter} of fiscal {fiscal_year}.

refusal.lesson.later_date: Why does it matter? Warren builds an estimate only from what was public on its date, and a forecast needs a few years of reports and market prices behind it. On an early date that history is too short, so a later date, when more of it has been published, will work.
refusal.lesson.earlier_date: Why does it matter? Warren uses only days that have ended in New York and whose market prices it has already downloaded, so that nothing in an estimate comes from after its date. The newest day it can use is a little behind today: pick that day or an earlier one.
refusal.lesson.company_data: Why does it matter? The company's reports up to this date leave out a figure the forecast needs, or give one it can't divide by, such as revenue of zero. Real filings have gaps like this (a line filed under a name Warren doesn't read, a quarter never reported on its own), so another date or another company usually works.
refusal.lesson.inconsistent_data: Why does it matter? Some facts about a balance sheet hold for every company: a balance the company holds or owes can't be below zero, and cash and short-term securities are part of current assets, so together they can't be larger than them. When a figure Warren read breaks one of these, it most likely belongs to a different measure, through the line Warren chose to read or the way it was tagged in the filing's data, so Warren refuses rather than value the company on it: open the report to compare its balance sheet, or try another date.
refusal.lesson.inconsistent_data.source: FASB, Concepts Statement No. 8, ch. 4; ARB 43, ch. 3A (now ASC 210-10-45-1)
refusal.lesson.no_value: Why does it matter? A DCF's terminal value adds up cash flows that grow forever, and that sum has a value only while the cost of capital is above zero and long-term growth stays below it; the familiar formula, next year's cash flow divided by the cost of capital minus growth, gives that sum. With the assumptions Warren reads from the data on this date one of those conditions fails, so the model has no value to show.
refusal.lesson.no_value.source: Gordon and Shapiro (1956); Damodaran, Investment Valuation, ch. 12
refusal.lesson.balance_item_negative: Why does it matter? Each balance sheet line Warren reads (cash, securities, current assets and liabilities, debt) is an amount the company holds or owes, so none can be below zero. A negative one most likely means a change or an adjustment was tagged as the balance, or Warren read a line meant for something else, so Warren refuses rather than guess which number was meant: open the report to compare, or try another date.
refusal.lesson.securities_exceed_current: Why does it matter? Short-term securities, and cash with them, are part of current assets, so together they can't be larger than current assets. When they are, a figure Warren read most likely holds a different measure (a total that also counts long-term holdings or restricted cash), or comes from an older balance sheet than the current assets it is set against. Warren refuses rather than count cash the company may not have: open the report to compare, or try another date.
refusal.lesson.erp_too_few_years: Why does it matter? Warren estimates how much more stocks earn than government bonds as the average of past years, and needs at least {min_years} full years of it. Stock returns swing by about {sd}% from year to year, so a {min_years}-year average has a standard error of about {se} percentage points, and with about 95% confidence the true premium could be up to {two_se} points higher or lower; a shorter window would be noisier still. A later date adds years.
refusal.lesson.setup: Why does it matter? Warren's own data for this estimate isn't there yet: a company's filings, its market prices, the Treasury rate, or a country's tax rate. This doesn't depend on you or the company; whoever runs Warren has to load it.
